tagline.text: A large cold-spring swimming pool fed by Mt. Mambajao in western Camiguin

location.label: Location
location.text: Mainit, Catarman, Camiguin, about 2.4 km inland from the coastal circumferential road

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: February–June and October on clear days

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱400~1,200 (per person, half day including entrance, transport and snacks)

children.text: Santo Nino Cold Spring is a large natural swimming pool in the interior of Catarman on the west side of Camiguin, filled by spring water from Mt. Mambajao. Locals put the water temperature at about 20℃, and it is a popular stop on the island loop to cool off, often paired with Tuasan Falls.
Sto. Niño Cold Spring lies inland in Barangay Mainit, Catarman, on the west side of Camiguin. It is about
2.4 km
inland from the coastal circumferential road, and one blog describes it as about
4 km

north of Catarman town proper, uphill. It is listed under this name on OpenStreetMap, at roughly 9.150 degrees north and 124.674 degrees east. Camiguin has a volcano at its heart, so hot springs, cold springs and waterfalls are plentiful, and this spot is often described as the largest cold-spring pool among them.

The water is said to flow down from Mt. Mambajao and keep welling up through the sandy bottom of the pool. It is therefore not still water but constantly refreshed, and some reviews say it is not chlorinated. I could not find an official temperature reading; locals say it is around
. On a near-equatorial island, the first few seconds at midday can take your breath away, but you quickly get used to it and feel refreshed.
The facilities are large and simple. The centerpiece is a big stone pool of about

, with a shallow children's pool right next to it where the water is said to feel even colder. Around the pools are picnic huts, tables, and shower and changing areas. Near the entrance, shops sell snacks and swimming gear. It is close to Tuasan Falls and Bura Soda Water Pool, so it fits naturally into a west Camiguin loop.

It is popular, so expect crowds. Bloggers report that the huts were nearly full on weekends and even on weekdays. To enjoy it in peace, aim for right after opening or a weekday morning, and if you want quiet rest more than swimming, you can reduce its share of your itinerary. The fees and hours below differ slightly by source, so please check locally before you go. Within a whole Camiguin loop, this is less a coastal-scenery stop than a swimming and resting place. Many visitors stay for half a day or more, spending the time swimming, napping and snacking, while those on a tight schedule stop for just an hour or so to cool off.
A large pool of about
; one review says you have to swim quite a way to reach the far side. Depth runs from about
at the edge to about
2 m
in the middle, though sources differ.

blocks.title: Spring welling up from the bottom

children.text: Water wells up from the sandy bottom, so fresh water keeps coming in. One review says it is clear enough to see swimmers' legs from across the pool.
Locals say it is about
. It is great for cooling off in the heat of the day, and a rash guard helps if you feel the cold easily.
There is a separate shallow pool beside the big one for kids. It is visible right from the entrance, and many families visit.
You can rent a hut around the pool to leave your belongings and rest. Many visitors bring snacks bought at the entrance shops and eat there.

Near the entrance, vendors sell snacks such as kiping (a thin, dried cassava-dough wafer drizzled with molasses, a Camiguin specialty). Many reviews say there is no restaurant inside the facility, so it is best to prepare food separately.
One review says non-swimmers can rent a buoy and float. Check availability and price on site.

blocks.title: A rest stop on the west loop

children.text: It fits well between
Tuasan Falls
and Bura Soda Water Pool. One blogger recommends spending the most time here of the three.
Leave your Mambajao accommodation by motorbike or multicab and ride west along the coastal circumferential road. It takes about
45 minutes
from Mambajao.
Stop first at Tuasan Falls or Bura Soda Water Pool. That way you can rest in the cold spring during the heat of midday.
Turn inland at Catarman and arrive at Santo Nino Cold Spring. Pay the entrance fee, claim a hut and swim in the big pool.
Buy snacks at the entrance shops and eat and rest in your hut. You can also have lunch at a restaurant in Catarman town.
Swim once more and then shower. Closing time is said to be 5 PM, so leave in good time.
On the way back to Mambajao, pass by the Sunken Cemetery and the Guiob church ruins.
One source says it opens at 11 AM on Mondays and Thursdays. If you arrive that morning, visit another place first and come in the afternoon.

items.title: Full-day west loop
items.subtitle: Cold spring, waterfall and sunken cemetery

children.text: Leave Mambajao and follow the west coastal road.
See the
Sunken Cemetery
and the Guiob church ruins. They lie between Mambajao and the cold spring.
Take a dip in the waterfall pool at
Tuasan Falls
Have lunch and look around Bura Soda Water Pool. Skip it if you are short on time.
Swim at length and rest at Santo Nino Cold Spring.
Return to Mambajao before sunset.
I could not confirm a direct flight from Manila to Camiguin Airport (CGM). Via Cebu you can use the Cebu–Camiguin route (Cebgo, about
50 minutes
), but seats are few and sell out early in peak season.
The more common route is a direct flight from Manila to Laguindingan Airport (CGY) in Cagayan de Oro (about
1 hour 30 minutes
), then overland and by boat.
From Laguindingan Airport to the Agora terminal in Cagayan de Oro takes about
1 hour
by shuttle, then about
1.5–2 hours
by bus from the terminal to Balingoan.
Flight fares and schedules change often, so check before booking.
The ferry from Balingoan port to Benoni port on Camiguin takes about
1 hour
, with a one-way fare of about
, plus a separate port fee.
Boats become fewer in the late afternoon, so it is safest to reach Balingoan by 3 PM at the latest.

items.title: Getting to the spring on the island

children.text: From Mambajao it takes about
45 minutes
by motorbike, and one blogger says Google Maps is enough. A motorbike rental runs around
a day.
Tricycles and shared multicabs also run, but public transport on the island is limited. From Catarman, follow the circumferential road, and when you see the spring's signpost, climb about
2.4 km
inland.
A day hire costs about
for a tricycle, while a multicab varies widely by source at about
. Agree on the price before you board.

To save money, take a shared multicab or jeepney from Mambajao to Catarman, then switch to a tricycle or motorcycle taxi (habal-habal). Transport back is hard to find, so settle your ride home in advance.
One review says the access road is a dirt track and dusty. You can park motorbikes near the entrance.
Sources say that
February–June
and
October
have relatively more clear days in Camiguin. Since this is a place for getting into cool water, a hot day at midday is best; rain can cloud the pool water, so pick a clear day.

Days and hours matter too. On weekends, holidays and in peak season (Holy Week, late March to May, the October Lanzones Festival, and year-end) huts are hard to get. For a quieter visit, go on a weekday morning.

During the day, it is easier on the body to see waterfalls or coastal sights in the morning and rest at the cold spring in the hot afternoon. Closing is said to be 5 PM, so it is hard to stay long after 4 PM.

There are not many good places to stay near the cold spring, so most visitors stay in Mambajao or near Benoni port and visit as a day trip. Catarman town also has accommodation, but it is small. The most common approach is to base yourself in central Mambajao or a coastal resort and do the west loop in one day. If you have rented a motorbike, it is easiest to leave early, spend the midday heat at the cold spring and return in the afternoon.

Many reviews say there is no restaurant inside the pool area; entrance shops sell drinks, snacks and kiping. It is easier to have lunch in Mambajao or Catarman town, or bring a packed meal. One older review mentions ordering from a restaurant and having it delivered to the table, but whether that is still possible is unknown. Many visitors eat snacks they brought in their hut. Camiguin is known for lanzones fruit, kiping and fresh seafood, so a safe plan is to snack lightly at the spring and eat proper meals in town.
Sources disagree on the entrance fee, at ₱50~75. Bring enough cash and check the ticket-booth sign.
One source says it opens at 11 AM on Mondays and Thursdays (8 AM–5 PM on other days). Hours can change, so check the latest announcement.
The water is very cold, so enter slowly at first, and wear a rash guard if you feel the cold.
If you cannot swim, ask on site whether buoys can be rented.
Combine it with Tuasan Falls and Bura Soda Water Pool in one trip to cut down on travel.
To avoid the crowds, go on a weekday morning and claim a hut as soon as you arrive.
Bring a towel, a change of clothes, sunscreen, water and a plastic bag. Entrance shops may be pricey.
A motorbike requires an international driving permit and a helmet.
If you bring children, claim a hut near the shallow pool so it is easy to watch them.
At midday the ground at the pool edge can be hot in the sun, so water shoes are helpful.
Depth reaches about 2 m in the middle but differs by source, and it is unknown whether life-saving equipment is sufficient. Keep a close watch on weak swimmers and children.
The water is very cold, so anyone with heart or blood-pressure concerns should acclimatize gradually and not overdo it.
The roughly 2.4 km access road to the entrance is a dirt track and can be slippery after rain.
The bottom is rocky, so only dive or jump in after checking that it is safe.
Leave valuables in your hut and do not leave the hut unattended.
Fees, opening days and hours differ by source, so follow the local notices.
It is about
15–25 minutes
by road, and one guide puts it at about
10 km
. It is the stop most often paired with the cold spring on the west loop.
Another natural pool close to the cold spring. One review says the fees are similar, and many say this one is quieter.
About
25 minutes
from the cold spring toward Mambajao, you will find the crosses of a cemetery sunk into the sea.
A hot spring heated by volcanic heat, in contrast to the cold spring, and good to pair with it on the same day.
